utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Before we hear the witness, are there any matters that the parties would like to bring to our attention?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there's just a couple of brief matters before it commences. The first of those is I'm advised by my learned friend that the Prosecutor has chosen to seek to proceed pursuant to 89(F) with this witness. Now, apart from a mild desire that we be -- well, a desire that we be told about these matters further in advance, I think in this case I'm told by the Prosecutor that effectively we have a misunderstanding about it. In fact, we have no objection to that course being taken in relation to this witness. It's an appropriate witness for that to happen. So I indicate that in advance. There are -- there are two other brief matters. The first concerns the provision of briefing notes. We're grateful for the briefing notes that we do get, but it's important that we get those promptly. It's been a little uneven so far. We do appreciate the efforts that are being made. We also appreciate that there are real life constraints on the Prosecutor about when they speak to a witness and so on. But we need to place on record that in order to properly prepare and to keep the cross-examination within limits, the more time we have, the more efficient we will be. So that I wish to make that point. Finally, Mr. Re was here a moment ago but now he's gone, Your Honour, there have been a number of witnesses that have sought protective measures up to this point. Now, it's been indicated to us that there is a particular witness who may or may not seek such measures in the future. Obviously nothing has been put to us to say that they're going to at this stage. But we want to indicate that in relation to that particular witness we will not -- Mr. Re is here now. Your Honour, might I just re-commence what I was going to say because he knows about this matter, it's best if he's here to respond. As Mr. Re is here I now indicate there was a witness in respect of whom it was indicated to the Defence sometime ago - I think over a week ago - that that witness may wish for protective measures. That indication - and the Prosecution can confirm that this is accurate - was given in this way, that it just wasn't clear whether the witness wanted them or not, and the Prosecution was going to indicate to us if the witness did want them. Now, I make it clear in respect of that witness - I'm not saying his name now - the Defence will not be consenting to that in the least, and we will contest it. And we want an opportunity to prepare to contest that. And we also indicate that we would not be satisfied in that regard with assurances from the bar table. That would have to be proved. That witness is a contentious and potentially important witness. So I just want to put it on record that should that witness indicate to the Prosecution that he wants protective measures, the Prosecution ought to tell us that immediately and give us due course. We cannot be put in the position of that being said on the morning, because that matter will be litigated and litigated hard. I mention that now so my learned friend knows that that matter stands and so that the Court -- so the Tribunal knows what's coming should such an application be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation concerning of the Prosecution's proposal for the proceeding in accordance with the Rule 89(F). And secondly, I believe that this witness was not sent back last week. So there's a possibility for the Prosecution to have the proofing notes as early as possible so as to inform the other parties about that. Mr. Weiner, would you like to clarify this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This witness arrived yesterday around 12.30 in the Netherlands, appeared in the office at approximately 2.30. We spoke to her until 5.30. And by approximately 6.00 we had the proofing notes faxed. They have a problem with their fax, so then we, I think, attempted to e-mail them, and in addition to that we also left hard copies in their box. We notified them and they said they would pick them up last night. Their fax has been down on and off for a week now, they've had trouble with their e-mailing. We took every possible option to get them. And I was also here throughout the night to provide them if there was a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that you have shown good course for the proofing notes. But as a principle in the future, as soon as the witness arrives in The Hague and you will prepare those proofing notes and furnish it to the Defence as early as possible. That's a principle. Another matter is protective measures. We also want to know beforehand what kind of protective measures you are going to request so that the Bench as well as the Defence could be very prepared. Well, it's a -- just a request from the Bench. Well, having said that, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is being collected, Your Honour, might I request of the Prosecution that we be told the witnesses at least for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that we have one the week before, but maybe there's some changes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's being prepared today, Your Honour..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You mean you could furnish it to the Defence today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Ms. Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do I hear the translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, madam.

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you state your name, please.

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Marija Definis-Gojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us how you're employed.

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm employed as a professional forensic pathologist in the clinical hospital in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Specifically which hospital or what's the location of that hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's the clinical hospital in Split in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you just tell us your educational history, please, just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I studied medicine and graduated in 1984. After working as a general practitioner for several years, I began to specialise in forensic medicine which I graduated in in 1992, and since then I have been working as a forensic specialist in the hospital I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to show you a document on the screen in front of you. It's Prosecution's 65 ter Exhibit list number 136, ERN number 01057280, and MFI number 166. We're going to Sanction right now and just show you page 1 of this. It begins with report number 188/94 and runs through reports 199/94. Are you familiar with these documents, ma'am -- or doctor?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what are they, these reports, please, in general?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The first page you showed, this is the front page. It is the front page of the jacket in which an autopsy report is enclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And are these a group of autopsy reports?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next page you showed, yes, this is an autopsy report inserted in that jacket. And the following pages you showed, this one and another one, these are the official forms provided for by the legislation in order to report a death.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you present when these autopsies were performed, this number 188 through number 199 in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I personally carried out some of these autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you involved in drafting these autopsy reports, some of them?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I drafted the autopsy reports for those autopsies which I myself conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was there another pathologist also conducting autopsies with you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague, Dr. Andjelinovic, also conducted autopsies, and he compiled his autopsy reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you present when all of these autopsies were conducted?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Because all these autopsies were carried out at the same time in an autopsy room, and they were all inspected and dealt with in a single day. We worked together each at our own table.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you review all of these remains or corpses? Did you at least observe them?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I looked at the bodies I myself dealt with, but my colleague and I cooperated in the following way. We would go over to each other's tables, look at what was happening, comment on it. That's how we cooperated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And have you reviewed these autopsy reports, yours as well as the ones performed or written by Dr. Andjelinovic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And having reviewed them, are these reports accurate?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What do you mean by asking are they accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, is the information contained in them true to the best of your knowledge, information, and belief?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is true. It was done, everything was done, according to the best of our knowledge and skill.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were these autopsy reports prepared for legal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When we did these autopsies, the purpose was exclusively to identify the bodies. That is how we dealt with the bodies and compiled the reports. At the time, we did not know that there would be any trials conducted in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to show you another autopsy report which you brought with you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I've just showed her, Your Honours, a report which is marked at the top 240/94.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Have you looked at that, ma'am? When was that autopsy performed in relation to the others that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Number 240/94 was carried out on the 23rd of June, 1994, precisely a month after the autopsies mentioned by the Prosecutor just minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the information -- first let's take a step back. Who performed that autopsy, the number 240/94?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I did personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who drafted or prepared the report that you have in your hands?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I drafted it, but it was probably typed out by my secretary because all the autopsy reports were typed out by the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the information contained in that report, is that true to the best of your knowledge, information, and brief?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to show you a copy of the statement which was -- which you gave to an Office of the Prosecutor investigator in 2002. Have you had a chance to look at those notes, doctor, that statement, doctor?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And have you read it or reviewed that statement?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is the information in that true to the best of your knowledge, information, and belief?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally I would like to show you the proofing notes from yesterday. Have you seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you provide the information contained in that document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And have you read it or reviewed it?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is the information true to the best of your knowledge, information, and belief that's contained in that document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the information contained in all of these documents, whether it's the proofing report, the statement, the autopsy reports, is this the information you planned to provide to this Chamber today?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, since the information that she planned to testify to today is all provided in these documents, we would like to introduce these documents pursuant to Rules 89(F) and 89(C) and turn the witness over for cross-examination at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, there may be an objection depending on the answers to the last of the documents, but all the others should be tendered in the way indicated and there's no objection to that. And it may be that I don't oppose the last document once I've asked some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe we could deal with this matter at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Morrissey, do you have any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I do. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. Doctor, I'm going to ask you some general questions first and then I'll ask you some questions about the specific cases that you had to deal with. First of all, the way in which you received the human remains which you had to analyse was not something that you were in control of but something that another agency was in control of bringing those bodies to the hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you have any role in supervising the way in which those bodies were stored or transported or handled generally by those agencies before they came to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just excuse me. I'm going to facilitate the ... I apologies for that. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And as to the information about where the human remains were retrieved from, you only know what you were told by those agencies or by family members or friends that you had a chance to speak to in the course of the analysis. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And therefore when on the autopsy report you record details such as place of death, you are doing that simply based upon what you were told by other individuals. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And quite frankly, it lay outside of your power then to verify whether that information was accurate. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And indeed it wasn't your job to look into whether or not that information was accurate. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think you've indicated this already that your purpose was not primarily or indeed -- I'll withdraw that question. I'll ask another one. In performing the autopsies that you did perform, your purpose was solely to identify the dead for official purposes and for the comfort of their families. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The main purpose was to establish the identity of the person and then if possible the cause of death, because we were duty-bound under the law after identifying the body to fill in the legal forms reporting death. And these require the cause of death to be entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to come to the way in which you arrived at or didn't arrive at causes of death in individual cases soon. All right. Now, the conditions -- perhaps, sorry, one more question about the receiving of bodies and that is this: It did happen from time to time that you would receive containers with parts of more than one body mixed in. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in some cases you would have more -- I'll come to that in a moment. Very well. Now, the next series of questions relate to the conditions under which you worked. You had a mortuary, I take it, with two tables operating simultaneously?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes there were more than two, depending on the number of bodies that came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. In normal civilian life you deal with autopsies normal -- ideally speaking in a thorough, slow, and painstaking way, taking up to two hours or sometimes even more over an individual case. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. How long were you able to allocate the individual human remains that you looked at in this case on the 23rd of May and then subsequently when you looked at the remains identified as Ivan Mandic about a month later?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you how many minutes or hours it was, but in any case, referring to the first group of bodies from numbers 188 to 199, these 12 bags, we probably had the whole day for our disposal and within that day all those bodies were looked at, identified, and all the forms filled in, and then the bodies were handed over to the relatives. How much time we spent on each particular body, I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. But it's the fact that you finished them all off in the one day.

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I have some questions for you about the process of identification. You had a policy only to release the remains to the family or to another person where there was a positive identification. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, under the then-prevailing conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And when deciding whether to release remains to a person, the only matter you really had to rely on was this -- was the individual certainty and conviction expressed by the family member or other person who had viewed the remains. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The conviction in the identity, yes, but not because the family member had viewed the remains, rather because the family member had studied the identifying elements, including information on clothing, footwear, objects found, anthropological data about gender, height, and so on, and any other identifying characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And you're right to correct me there. Because the person doing the identifying was entitled to have regard to a large range of possible identifying features. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But in the end it was the certainty of the identifier and not your satisfaction about that person's certainty which determined the release of the remains to that person. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ultimately it's always the person who is to identify the body who decides whether to accept the identification or not. It's not up to the doctor to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And particularly that -- the answer you've just given I take it was particularly true in a time of war where there was a high turnover of such remains and you really had a lot of people in that situation to deal with. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. With the leave of Their Honours, I would like to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, feel free.

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with your question as to how long the processing of the remains lasted, I have to say that this was done in a clinical hospital, as you have heard, in a hospital which has its patients, in a city which has its dead. So we had to deal both with the hospital cases, the normal city cases that would have occurred in peacetime, as well as the war victims brought in from the field. And this limited the amount of time we could spend on dealing with each body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. If your hospital had endless resources and endless pathologists to deploy those resources, there is technology in existence that allows for the identification even of quite damaged remains, and I'm speaking of DNA technology now. Given the state of the human remains that you encountered on this occasion, would it have been possible to embark upon DNA analysis and comparative analysis between the deceased on the one hand and family members on the other hand to see whether some sort of DNA match could be obtained in respect of those? And of course I am speaking hypothetically here, but I am asking you whether that is a possible thing that could happen.

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not hypothetical. The only problem is that in 1994 when these bodies were being processed, nothing was known of DNA. This method had not been introduced yet in our hospital; it was introduced several years later. Were this happening today, then these bodies would certainly have been subjected to DNA identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. Very well. Okay. Thank you for that. Now, just a couple more questions about the information that's on the sheets there -- that is on the autopsy reports, I should say. With respect to those, you have indicated -- rather than asking you a general question, I shall ask you about specific cases, so just excuse me now. Thank you. Doctor, I'm going to ask you about some of the specific cases now, and if you need to look at the notes, please feel free to do so, but I'll be working through your statement in asking the questions that I ask. Now, I want to take you first of all to the registered case 191/94. In this case, these remains were identified by the child of the deceased. You've noted in your statement that you have no idea of the cause of death. I want to ask you about the time of death. What is the range of potential times that the individual identified as Ivan Zadro might have died, given the state of what you had before you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult to answer this question in view of the state of the remains. There was putrefaction going as far as skeletisation, so it's difficult to establish the time of death. In any event, these were not fresh corpses, they were old corpses. Whether they had been buried, were in coffins, whether in the soil directly, all of this would influence the speed of these changes of the putrefaction, so it's impossible to say. In any case, they had been dead for quite a long time, but whether it was several months or a year, it's hard to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think you've anticipated some questions I was going to ask you. But once a body reaches the stage you found case 191/94 to be, it's just impossible to give anything more than a very general estimate as to what the minimum time was that the person had been dead for?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in this case the best you can do really is to say this person must have been dead for some months?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. I want to take you to the next case, number 192/94. This person was identified as Zivko Dreznjak. In this case you've noted a defect on the skull, but noted also that it's not an indicator of death or even of the timing of the skull defect. Is your position about the timing of the death of this individual the same as it was in relation to the previous one I asked you about, namely this person must have been dead for some months but you can't say anymore?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. As in the previous case, the same applies to all these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And really it was impossible in relation to any of them to establish a cause -- an actual cause of death. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm going to jump forward to one individual, and if you go to case 240/94, this is a person identified as Ivan Mandic who was brought to the hospital on the 23rd of June. Do you have your notes about that? This was one which you brought a separate report along to court about.

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In your statement you noted that the description in the report corresponds partially to photographs attached to the case. Now, what did you mean by that phrase "corresponds partially"? Did you mean that there's some areas that don't match or -- perhaps I'll leave it to you. What did you mean by that phrase?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I had in mind when I wrote this, I really can't say now why it says "partially" here. It does correspond to the photographs. The only thing is that on the photographs you can see more than is evident from the record. This may be the reason why I inserted "partially."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Do you have present in court with you a folder of photographs which were taken during the time of the autopsies that you performed?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not have the same set of photographs that you have, but I have the originals with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Could I ask you -- if you have the originals with you, could I ask you, please, to produce the originals of the case number 240/94, the person identified as Ivan Mandic. Could I inquire, do you have those present in the Tribunal room here right this moment or not?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Would you just mind holding up those photographs and displaying them so I can identify that I have the same ones that you have. Could I just ask you to identify -- we're going to put them on a display in a moment. Could you just identify please -- they're on the display now; you've anticipated me. Thank you. Very well. Could you just identify them one by one. The photograph that's on the screen now, what does that depict?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is a skull marked as S-240/94.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Would you just display one after the other the photographs that you have relevant to that case only at this stage, please.

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] That's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Could you identify -- that's another part of the same material?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now you're displaying a third photograph -- I have to say it out loud for the record, doctor. You're now displaying a third photograph which indicates bones belonging to the same item. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. These are the bones as they were brought, whereas the previous photograph depicted the skeleton that was composed of those bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. You're now showing a fourth photograph. Does that depict certain items of clothing that were associated with that skeleton?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Those are pieces of clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can you move on to the next one, please.

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What is the next one? I have two more, but they are similar if not identical to the ones we've seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think for completeness perhaps we can just identify them. That again is a photograph of skeletal bones associated with that item?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And finally -- and the sixth is a photograph depicting clothes once again?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I offer those for tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In relation to those remains that you've noted there, it is the case that no cause of death could be identified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, just one thing. We have no objection to allowing those photographs to being tendered; however, those are part of her own records, if we could make copies of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be perfectly satisfied with that course as long as the Court sees no difficulty with it. Can I indicate that the Prosecution were good enough to provide us with some enlarged copies. And the question is not to going to descend to a level of detail where the picture quality matters in a massive way. So I'd be satisfied with that, as long the Court has no difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, of course, on our part there is not difficulty at all. The only issue that -- after that copy, I hope the parties could meet with the Court Deputy to find out the proper numbers for those, you know, documents so that later on we could find out them very easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That will be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. I'm sorry. I was going to ask you about the cause of death and then I can't remember if I got the answer or not, but I think -- the question was: There was no cause of death able to be established in relation to this individual. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And looking to that, what you've got there, that individual could just have easily have died from shooting, stabbing, clubbing to death, or a heart attack. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In theory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. I'll return back to the chronological list of persons, and I'd ask you now to consider case 188/94, remains identified as Ruza Maric. With respect to placing a time on that -- on the death of that person, I take it the same answer is applicable, namely that you can say this person had been dead for some months but you can't say any more than that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And is it correct to say the same in respect to cases 194/94, 195/94, 196/94, 197/94, 198/94, and 199/94?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In all of these cases, the same applies: The cause of death could not be determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I've got a question for you about the contemporaneity of the deaths of all the individuals you saw. Could I put this proposition to you: You can't comment on whether or not they died at or around the same time, is that accurate, based of course on your expert analysis rather than external information?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Based only on our findings, I cannot say that they died at the same time, but I can say equally that it is possible they found their deaths at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Just excuse me a moment. I may have some residual questions and then we'll be finished. The use of the phrase in the autopsy report "violent death of unknown cause," which is to be seen in some of the reports is not a pathological finding but a description suitable to that form based upon external information outside of your field of expertise. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that diagnosis which runs through all these cases, violent death of unknown cause, you find it in each of these reports, contains this word "violent." Violent death is a term that does not in itself designate the cause of death, so it shouldn't be here in a manner of speaking. But it was written there because we were talking about casualties, victims of war, and it is assumed that each one of them died a violent death. But I agree with you, that brings us no nearer to the cause of death from a medical point of view. Or, with your leave, I would like to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The forms attached to the reports entitled "the registration of the fact of death" contain a column, a rubric titled "information on the cause of death." The law envisages three cases: Homicide, suicide, and violent and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the third one was not caught by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of these qualify as violent death. And that is the only reason why we used this, especially in the Latin version, "mors violenta," violent death. In other words, we pathologists were not in a position either then or now to establish which kind of death it was. Death by misadventure was the third category, homicide, or suicide. I know you are very familiar with this. So there were three categories of violent death: Homicide, suicide, and accident or death by misadventure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And the designated category in this case was the third one -- sorry, pardon me. I'll ask you the question again because there was a difficulty with the interpretation earlier on. The term that is used -- that you used -- just excuse me. I just want to put it to you accurately. The term "violent death of unknown cause" is a pro forma term used on the forms as one of a limited number of legal alternatives that's allowed to you to fill out the form. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are the questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-direct, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, doctor, you indicated it was possible that all of these people died at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Based on your training and experience, could these persons have died in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's very possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, there was some discussion with regard to certainty of identification of remains by family members, and you mentioned that in addition the family member you also rely on anthropological data. Can you please explain what the reliance is on anthropological data.

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Anthropological data for the purposes of our discussion relate to identifying age, gender, height, and in our case not race because there is only a single race in our territory, plus certain features such as old fractures, deformities, and things like that. There are certain anthropological methods that are applied in order to determine age, gender, and all the other elements that I mentioned. If you wish a more precise answer, I can enumerate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you one question. With regard to gender or sex, by looking at those skeletal remains, whether it's the skulls or the other bones in each of those bodies, can you determine whether those remains belong to a man or a woman?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Of course I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So if you see in front of you the remains of a male or a man and some family member comes in and says, That is my sister, those are the remains of my sister, what action do you take? Do you turn the body over --

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then of course we would not agree on this identification. I'm speaking hypothetically of course. It could happen that a female can bear some male characteristics or a man can bear some female characteristics. A man can be short, have a broad pelvis, has lumps on the bones, et cetera, in which case certain additional methods are used to achieve a positive identification of sex or gender. So we confront the family member or we give them additional anthropological elements on the basis of which it can be proven that one or the other is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So basically in addition to an individual's identification of a family member, you also use other scientific means to confirm that identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: First of all, it's a leading question and secondly it's turning a positive -- getting a positive out of the negative. I think the thrust of what the witness was saying was that she would decline to accept an identification in certain terms, not that she would scientifically confirm one. And so I object both to the form and the substance of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: To me there's no problem with this question because, you know, we have to give the witness an opportunity to explain what is in her mind. Of course the witness is an expert; she has the full right to agree with the Prosecution or disagree with them. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question is basically: In addition to an individual's identification of a family member, do you also use scientific methods to corroborate that identification?

utterances.speaker: MARIJA DEFINIS-GOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will start from the beginning. The main methods of identification - and we will not be speaking now of highly sophisticated scientific methods as DNA matches - we are talking now about basic identification methods. What are they based on? They are based on comparing data provided by the family with data obtained by clinical examination of a dead body. If this data coincide, we get a positive identification; if they do not coincide, it is a negative identification. It is a fact that an identification is not based on a single element; it is based on a whole complex, a whole set of elements. Therefore, a person cannot be identified only by finding a wallet that the family recognised as the wallet of their family member, of their loved one. A whole series of identification elements have to coincide to provide for a positive identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage are there any documents to tender? Mr. Weiner, would you please read out the numbers of those documents again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: While my friend is doing that, Your Honour, I indicated a potential objection to the last of the four; I withdraw that objection in light of the answers given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The first document or set of documents are the autopsy reports, which is number 136 on our Prosecution 65 ter list which has the ERN of 0105-7280 and it runs through 7353. So 0105-7280 through 0105-7353.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. What's the MFI number?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Court Deputy, do you have it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 166, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: MFI 167 is the witness's statement and proofing notes. The -- which would be MFI 167.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then the third or the final document is the additional autopsy report 240/96 which at this point does not -- I'm sorry, 240/94 which at this point does not have an ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is it possible for it to have an MFI number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, that can be included with MFI 166 and scanned accordingly, so it will have one MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I guess there's no objections from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Those documents are admitted into evidence. On the part of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, we would seek to tender as a single exhibit the bundle of paragraphs which would tendered as MFI 168, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Morrissey, that would be MFI 168.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I hope for each photograph there is -- should be some ID numbers. For instance, the slash 1, slash 2 or slash A, slash B, so we can know what document it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to procedure, all documents brought into the Tribunal are ERNd. What I can do is have ERN numbers placed on those photographs when they are finally prepared, as well as the final autopsy report which may help the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But an ERN number is so complicated. Sometimes it is very difficult to remember, so I prefer the slash 1, slash 2, these kinds of things. I'm entirely in the hands of the Court Deputy to do that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Weiner and I as two counsel could easily make a mess of it but we'll do what we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. I believe that your expert testimony is very helpful to this case. And after we adjourn, the usher will show you out of the room and we wish you a very pleasant journey back home. And after that we'll hear the next witness I guess. And we'll take our break for 25 minutes and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as for the next witness, I guess there's no protective measures? Yes, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I didn't hear the translation. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Ms. Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good morning. Is your name Erdin Arnautovic?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Nickname Dino?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you were born on the 13th of September, 1958?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your occupation is a taxi driver?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you a series of questions. Is it correct that you did no JNA military service after you left school because of a disability?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You're not a member of a political party now nor during the war?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In April 1992, you joined the Green Berets and the Patriotic League at about the time hostilities started in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Later that year in about June you joined the 3rd Mountain Brigade which later merged with the 9th Motorised Brigade, which was part of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The corps commander of the 1st Corps command was Vahid Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were a soldier involved in the defence in Sarajevo from the outset and you were wounded, shot in the knee in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were in hospital or hospitalised for at least ten days?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: After that you were given a role in logistics?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The commander of the 9th Motorised Brigade was Sulejman Imsirovic?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The deputy commander was Ramiz Delalic, nickname Celo?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Celo means "bold" in Bosnian; it can also mean head or main guy or boss?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he had hair on his head, but they still called him Celo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you call him?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: I called him Ramiz or Celo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And do you regard him as a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in 1993 were you in working -- sorry, was your role as a logistics officer in the assault unit which was personally commanded by Ramiz Delalic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That contained a proposition that the assault unit was personally commanded by Ramiz Delalic, and that's the sort of information that can't be led but needs to be asked in a proper way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe we are at the stage of going step by step at this sage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll take you back a step, Mr. Arnautovic. Was there an assault unit within the 9th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you in that?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you its logistics officer?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was the commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: In that period, it was Malco Rovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: After that when we went to Grabovica, it was Zuti, Zuti was his nickname. I didn't know his real name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which leads right to going to Grabovica. In September 1993 before you went to Grabovica, where were you stationed?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you learn that you were going to go to Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Corps Vahid Karavelic summoned us and lined us up in front of our command. They gave us the order that we were to set out toward Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did he say to you -- sorry. I withdraw that. How many people were lined up and what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: About 120 men were lined up and he read out an order that we were to go to Jablanica and we would be put under Zuka's command there. He would be in charge of the operation and we would apply to him for whatever we needed. We were given some weapons, some lunch packages, and some cigarettes when we set out toward Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he tell you what the operation was that you would be involved in?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Liberating Mostar. We were to go in the direction of Mostar to liberate that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the size of the brigade? How many men were in the 9th Motorised Brigade and the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: In the brigade there were about 5.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the process by which 120 people came to be lined up before the 1st Corps commander? How were they chosen?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: We were told to take reconnaissance men and sabotage men from each unit, men who were sappers and so on, and to take four or five men from each unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say "from each unit," do you mean from the 1st Corps or the 9th?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: The 9th Motorised.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the 10th Brigade, that's Adnan Solakovic's -- I'm sorry, the 2nd Independent Brigade. Were there soldiers from there in that line-up as well? That's Adnan Solakovic's brigade.

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: They arrived there before us. And when we arrived there, we found them in Grabovica, and the 10th Mountain who were in Jablanica and some other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Commander Karavelic tell you how you were to get to Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: When you pass through the tunnel, we would be met by trucks in Hrasnica and from there we would be transported by truck as far as Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You're referring to the tunnel under Sarajevo airport?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What day was that that he lined you up in front of the -- lined you up and gave you these orders?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: It was the 7th. I know it was night. It was at about 7.00 p.m. When we were lined up in front of our command in Trapo Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you leave for Grabovica that same night?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you in fact met by trucks?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived, we had problems about transportation in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were those problems resolved?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We called for Ramiz Delalic to come to Hrasnica and see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As a result of that, did trucks arrive and did you leave for Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many trucks were required to transport the group of soldiers to Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Three trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you drive through the night?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there any incidents -- did any incidents occur along the way between your soldiers and police at checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I object to this. Your Honour, if this is a matter that's supposed to be within the knowledge of Mr. Halilovic, it might conceivably be relevant. If it's just an incident concerning this individual and police or people from that unit and police, then it's irrelevant, and I object to the question on the grounds of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. What's the relevance of this piece of evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The relevance goes strictly and only to this: I anticipate the witness will say there was an incident which was reported in a report by the police which gives a date, and the date is on the report. It only goes to the date being the date of this witness and his men leaving Sarajevo and arriving in Grabovica. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry. Well, Your Honour, the witness has given a direct, clear answer as to when the date was that he left, and there's no need for him to be shown any document unless there be some basis for him -- that he was the author or something of that nature or saw the document at the time. At the moment he's given a clear answer, and it seems both irrelevant and also unnecessary establish what my friend says the purpose of it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The question is if you have any disputes. If there's none, then we have settled it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Arnautovic, what time -- approximately what do you mean did -- I withdraw that. You said you drove through the night to get to Grabovica. Did you go somewhere before you got to Grabovica? Where did you stop en route?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: We had problems in a place called Pazaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Moving on from there, where did you stop next?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: We stopped in Jablanica next.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At what time did you go to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: We got there in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it light or dark?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: It was already light. It was daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long was it after dawn? Can you give an approximate time of when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: It was around 8.00 a.m. approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did anyone meet you, this is your group of soldiers, when you got there?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were met by Zuka's logistics and Zuka's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where was that? Where did you meet them?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: In front of Zuka's headquarters in Gornja Jablanica, I think it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about Zuka? You said your orders were that you were to become commanded by Zuka when you got to Grabovica. Did you meet Zuka? ?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What's his name? That's his nickname; what's his full name?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know it at the time, but later I learned it was Zulfikar Alispago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you meet him on arrival or at some later point?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely, but he stayed there, he slept there, he was there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about his deputy? Did he have a deputy, and if so did you meet his deputy?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was his deputy's name and when did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Nihko, Nihad. That was his name as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: That day I met many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did Zuka or his men tell you when you got to Jablanica -- Zuka's base in Jablanica about what you were to do and where you were to go and so on?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: We were told we would be billeted in Jablanica, but however they then told us to go on to Grabovica and that we would be billeted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they say who you would be billeted with in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't tell us right away. They just said everything had been taken care of. We didn't even know there would be some sort of population there and that they would be living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you aware at that time when you first arrived at Zuka's base whether or not there were any ABiH units then in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that some other units had arrived there before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Jablanica for approximately?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: An hour or two perhaps so that the fighters could have a rest, and then we went to accommodate ourselves in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: By truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did anyone meet you when you went to -- when you arrived in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Adnan Solakovic's men were there and some others, and then we were told to find accommodation in those houses. I don't know what Zuka's main logistics man was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who told you to find accommodation in those houses and which houses are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in that village there were houses there; I can't say how many. We were told to find accommodation there. They said everything would be all right and there would be no problems; however, when the men went to find accommodation, there were local people there who opposed their staying in those houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said "we were told to find accommodation," were you referring then to the men at Zuka's base telling you to find accommodation at Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They said everything had been taken care of and agreed with the local people and that there would be no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you do, you personally, to find accommodation for the men who were with you when you arrived in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: I was near Adnan Solakovic's house where his men where; I was across the road from there. And when people started finding accommodation, they came back and said, Nobody wants us there in those houses. And then I said, We'll see what the problem is when these main men arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just said "when people started finding accommodation," are you referring to the soldiers who came with you on the trucks?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just said "nobody wants us there in those houses." Who is the nobody that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: The local people who lived in those houses. They didn't want to take anyone in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was their ethnicity or nationality?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: They were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you told why they didn't want to take members of the ABiH in?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, allegedly the people from the corps who had been there had agreed that they would put us up, but there was some sort of misunderstanding about our accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you able to find accommodation for yourself and your men?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, excuse me, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: He hasn't said that he had any men at this stage and if it's to be suggested that he -- the witness was in command of some men or had men under his control, then the Prosecutor ought to lead that evidence before he states it and puts it to the witness as a fact built into a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe the men means the people because the witness said that when people started finding accommodations. Then a question asks: "Are you referring to soldiers who came with you on the trucks."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that, Your Honour, but it's the next section that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can rephrase it. I don't mean they're under his command, but I can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Arnautovic, were you able to find accommodation for yourself and that group of soldiers that arrived with you in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: I found an empty house for myself and a group, and another group was accommodated above where we were when Vehbija Karic and five or six others arrived to check what was going on and whether we had found accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Go on. I withdraw that. You said you found an empty house. Why did you choose this empty house for yourself?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because of the ammunition and all that, food, cigarettes so I could store it all and not have people take it and carry it off because there was a meadow there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it your responsibility as the logistics officer to look after these supplies?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that a house in which you felt you would be able to secure those logistics supplies?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to show the witness Exhibit P3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Arnautovic, just have a look at the screen in front of you. Do you recognise that as a photograph of the village of Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I want you to do is with a pen, I want you to mark several things on it. First of all, can you see in that photograph the place where your trucks of men arrived on the morning of the 8th of September, 1993? Firstly I'm asking you, can you see it before I ask you to mark. Can you see the place where the trucks arrived?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see the house where you stored your logistics supplies?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Can you please circle -- sorry, place a 1 in the place where the trucks arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It appears not to be working, Your Honour. If it's a technical problem requiring resolution, I can always return to his marking of two photographs at a later point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Arnautovic, so you know what I'm going to do, I'm going to ask you to mark on this photograph and another one the place where the bus arrived -- or sorry, the trucks arrived; the place where you stayed, the house you secured; and the houses in which other soldiers stayed. But we'll come back to that. You --

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Am I supposed to mark this?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not just yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, you referred earlier to some commanders or I think you said main men arriving in Grabovica. I want you to just tell the Trial Chamber what happened before they arrived. You said you went looking -- you went looking for accommodation, you found one house. What about the other soldiers? Did they -- which houses did they stay in or find? There was a house where some soldiers had found accommodation and the rest were unable to find accommodation. So they began to complain and a problem arose because they didn't know where they would sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And on the photograph which should still be on the screen, can you see the houses there where soldiers managed to find somewhere to stay?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: This was the house where I was put up. The other soldiers were here. In this house lower, down here, was Solakovic's. And then there were other houses in which other soldiers were placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said the soldiers began to complain. Who did they complain to?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: They came to complain to me. They said, We have nowhere to sleep. How are we going to be accommodated? There's nothing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your response?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: I said, Well, let's see. I'll go to see Zuka and see what the problem is, why there is know accommodation for us. Shortly after that, four or five of them came, among them Mehmed Karic who said that he was the one in charge, that they had taken care of accommodation. And when my men started rumbling and saying there was no actually accommodation available, he said, Don't you pay attention to those who tell you no. Anyone who says a word against it will be thrown into the Neretva summarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This Karic you just mentioned, what was his position or his rank; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, he had a higher rank because he served in the former army and he brought his former rank with him. I think he was in the artillery or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know how high his rank was?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think they assigned rank to each other or assumed ranks at will. I think it was only in 1997 that ranks were actually distributed properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where was it that you had this meeting with Mr. Karic and the others?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: We met up in front of this house where I was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's certainly not the witness's fault and it's not Mr. Re's fault either. The difficulty is we can't see where the witness is indicating, so it's a bit difficult for us to follow what's happening here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll produce a hard copy photograph and put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe that's the best way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Re, you may ask the witness to mark on that hard copy, and later on we'll have it scanned into the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will do. For the record, I'm going to show the witness photographs P3 and Exhibit P7, 0149-4608 and 4612. While we're finding the hard copies, I'll move on. I will get back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many of the soldiers were with you when Mr. Karic spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: There were over a hundred soldiers including Adnan Solakovic's soldiers because everybody was keen to hear what was going to be said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Describe how the soldiers were grouped in relation to Mr. Karic and the people with him.

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: He was standing right outside the house and the soldiers made a semicircle around him, around the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said there were four or five in his group and you said that Mr. Karic was of a high rank or a high-ranking person. Were those people with him also high ranking?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, they were from the corps and I think I remember it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they have any uniforms or insignia or anything to signify to you what rank they may have had or the position they may have had within the corps?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they had insignia of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but at that time I don't remember anybody had any ranks. And it simply worked this way: If you were in the corps, then you were of a higher rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You mean by that that the people with Mr. Karic appeared to you to be of high rank. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: It's not that it appeared to me. I know that they had a high rank in the corps and in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When Karic was addressing you and you were speaking to him, were you paying attention to who these other ranking people from the corps were?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: At that time I wasn't really paying attention to memorise who was there. I was rather paying attention to what was being said and I was trying to find the logic of putting up us there together with camp inmates from western Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Right. Returning to the photographs now, is the on-screen marking now working? Okay. If you could please look at photograph Exhibit P3 -- in fact, I think we're being shown P7. I want you to mark with a 1 the place where the trucks arrived.

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: You mean on both photographs? There are two them, one here and one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just make that a little bit larger, please, and maybe put a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I want you to mark with a 2 and also a circle the house which you secured for yourself.

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Maybe you could put the 2 outside the circle with an arrow leading to it so it's clear.

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And with a 3, the house where Adnan Solakovic's men were staying.

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You also mentioned another house where his men were. Can you mark that with a 4 please.

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: You mean another house where Adnan Solakovic's soldiers were located? Adnan was there in that house at the entry to Grabovica, and this is the house where his soldiers were put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the one with a number 3?

utterances.speaker: ERDIN ARNAUTOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we now turn please to photograph Exhibit P7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry, just before -- I don't want to cause trouble here. On my screen here, the number 3 didn't appear where the witness was going to mark the number 3 in relation to where he says Solakovic's men were at. We have got a 2 marked clearly, and then we lose the 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. On my screen I didn't see it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Perhaps it was just an oversight. Perhaps if the witness marks a 3 and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Could we try that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's just disappeared. We'll start the whole thing again, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
